utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd simply like to inform the Court that Dr. Helena Ranta is still here and in the public gallery and should I work on the assumption that the Court wishes her to remain here during the morning? She has rescheduled her flight to return to Finland this evening so she can be here if the Trial Chamber wishes her to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If Dr. Ranta wishes to leave, she may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, good morning. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were reviewing some of the forensic work that was done regarding the bodies of victims who were found at Racak, and I'd like to move to another part of the Racak area, the area that is known usually either as the gully or the ravine. And I apologise if I didn't warn Mr. Prendergast earlier that we needed the poster brought in, but it's almost here. And Professor Dobricanin, if you look at the aerial photograph the gully or ravine in this courtroom or at least on that courtroom is often referred to as crime scene -- or crime location number 5, and you see the 5 there with some arrows pointing along what looks to be a path over the mountain there. Do you see that, just to get oriented?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph taken of the bodies in the gully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, again this morning I'm going to be referring to a lot to Exhibit 156, tab 12, which is the full report of the European Union Forensic Expert Team. The first photograph is sort of a long overview shot of the bodies, some of the bodies lying in the gully. Mr. Prendergast, perhaps you could take three at one time just to save you from having to walk back and forth. Photo number 24, I believe, from the expert report. If that could go on the ELMO. And again, this is simply to get everyone oriented. This is from an area higher up on the gully obviously towards what appear to be a group of bodies lying in the gully. We see along the edge of the gully just bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see all that, Dr. Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'd like to draw your attention to a particular body that's -- right now that's lying in that group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could see the next photograph, please. I believe it's number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at it photograph. This is more of a close-up of this group of bodies. Professor Dobricanin, you see that they are marked with the kinds of numbers that were used during your autopsies: RA3 in the top right; RA35 going counter clockwise; RA15, et cetera. Do you see the body lower down in what sort of looks to be a maroon-coloured jacket? It's marked Racak 24. Do you see that body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that body, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Also, if you could just note as we're going through these photographs, above body number 24 we see body 21, and body 21 appears to be wearing a very light-coloured jacket. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we move a bit up and to the right we see body 3, who also is apparently wearing a very light-coloured jacket. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the next photograph, please, Mr. Prendergast, just to get a slightly different view. And if -- thank you very much, Mr. Technician. If we could move the photograph down just a little bit. No, down, please. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, Professor Dobricanin, you see the body. It's now at the top of this photograph which is photograph number 27 of the expert report, and again we see Racak 24 above that same body. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a man named Fatmir Limani, who died on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Exhibit C1, Your Honours, page 11, which is the statement that Dr. Helena Ranta provided to this Chamber upon this Chamber's request, Dr. Ranta explains that there were two molars found in the soil in the vicinity of this body in that position at the gully in a depth of about three to five centimetres, "in a position of victim Racak 24." And if I could also direct the Court's attention to appendix -- appendix 3, I believe of the European Union's full report. This contains results of DNA analysis. And we can find there reports explaining that a particular molar can be associated with the DNA of body Racak 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there is another photo that I need to show you, Professor Dobricanin, if I can find it quickly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Prendergast. This is page number 20 of the -- of appendix 1 of the expert report. It's ERN K0202330. If we could place that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: According to the report of the forensic expert team, Professor, this document or this page portrays the bodies that were found in this position in the gully, and it also portrays in little blue squares - they're hard to see, the colours seem to be hard to see on the monitor that I'm looking at - little blue squares indicate where bullets or bullet fragments were found when the gully was examined in November of 1999. And the red squares, small little red squares which we see primarily outside the gully where we saw bushes on the previous photograph, indicate where cartridge cases were found in November 1999 by the Finnish Expert Team. Now, I'm just wondering if you could comment, Professor Dobricanin, given the information that I've just shown to you, we have the body of RA24, Fatmir Limani, there in the gully. A bullet or part of a bullet as well as a tooth with the same DNA as Mr. Limani are found in the soil beneath the spot where Mr. Limani's body was found. Can we then conclude, Professor, that Mr. Limani was most likely shot where he lay?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to give you the same answer that I gave yesterday. Had we entered Racak on the 15th of January and had we found the bodies where they had been -- maybe it was in this spot, too, I'm not pre-judging anything. We found heaps of casings along the trenches. Had we carried out a normal investigation like in any other country in the world where the entire scene is sealed off, and there were possibilities for that because there were many verifiers and monitors there, today I could give you a concrete answer to a concrete question. Everything that you're saying now ask not be accepted or, rather, I cannot accept as absolutely certain, because only on the basis of the bodies that were photographed here, on the basis of markings of the bodies, these numbers, I mean, we cannot compare the bodies we autopsied to the bodies that are marked and numbered here. That is a very thankless and very uncertain job. These piles of casings could perhaps indicate that this was indeed the scene and that all the injuries came from the same direction, which absolutely was not the case. The distribution of casings shows something completely different in relation to what the true picture was. And then these teeth that are found, if the pulp is not there there can be no proper DNA analysis. Everything can be doctored. I'm a person who accepts only facts. My facts are absolutely on the side of the fact that it is a big-time mistake that we did not carry out the investigation on the spot on the very day. And again I put the question why we were not allowed access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like, if possible, to be assisted with the answer to this question. I think Mr. Saxon posed the question on the basis that these facts are correct. Now, they may not be correct. As you say, there may have been things tampered with. But one of the allegations you've -- one of the qualifications you've included in that answer is that there was not a complete-enough quantity of material for DNA. Now, that seems to suggest fabrication on the part of the Finnish Expert Team. Is that what you're suggesting? I was hoping that you would answer the question on the basis that let's accept that this is an accurate finding. What can we conclude from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Bonomy, I cannot conclude anything on the basis of things I had not seen myself. I'm a forensic doctor who knows how to reconstruct the scene on the basis of what he sees on the scene, not only on the basis of photographs that are blurred. Please do not misunderstand me. I am not devaluating anybody here. I have high regard for my colleagues from Finland, but this is a photograph that did not allow a professor of forensic medicine to give unequivocal answers to questions put in this way. It's as simple as that. As for the teeth and the DNA, the method applied was absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why was it you said if there was -- if there was no pulp there there could not be a proper analysis? Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that because pulp has to be there. If a tooth is broken or smashed with a projectile, it is virtually impossible to extract enough material from it to carry out a DNA analysis. However, I accept that if they had a complete tooth they could absolutely carry out this kind of analysis. However, again, on the basis of everything that I've been telling you, this doesn't mean anything to me. The only thing that is meaningful to me is what I see myself on the scene had I entered the place on the 15th of January. Whenever bodies are moved there are other elements involved. I do not recall the white jackets that are depicted here. I really do not recall any white jackets on the bodies of the persons from Racak who were autopsied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin, before you mentioned the pulp, you also said that "The distribution of casings shows something completely different in relation to what the true picture was." I couldn't follow that. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you see no casings in the background of this picture, if this is the true picture - again, I'm speaking very conditionally. I'm only speaking on the basis of a hypothesis, something that I did not see - had the direction of the shooting been there towards the bodies that were there. In order to have bullet paths from here to here, then the paths would go either from the back or from the front. We would not have bullet paths coming from the bottom upwards or from the top downwards, and we would not have anything that was slanted. That is the picture that is here. Casings are not a trace of anything else unless they were just put there on purpose. I'm not saying that, but if they were fired from automatic or semi-automatic weapons, I'm saying what the situation would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon, let me be clear. The Finnish team must have drawn this picture based upon the pictures taken on the 15th and 16th. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to clarify one or two points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Prendergast, I need to ask for your assistance again. This is a diagram. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please. Again produced by the Finish Expert Team. It's page 83 of appendix 2 to their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at this, please, Professor Dobricanin, this is a computer simulation of the terrain along that gully. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't see any trenches there along that gully, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gully resembles a kind of a trench. That's what it looks like to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a shallow kind of a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I may have misspoken earlier, so just so that the record is clear, I want to show you a photograph of a little bit of clothing. It is the first item of clothing taken from the body of victim 3 who we saw in a photograph earlier in the gully. I have may have misspoke be by referring to a white jacket. It may simply be a white or light-coloured pullover, but there it is. This was the first item taken off the body when this victim was autopsied according to the Finnish report. I don't know if you have any comment to make about this, Professor Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a comment. This is grey-coloured. Perhaps the picture is too light, but in the upper photograph it's a bit darker than on the lower photograph, and it's not the same colour as shown on the previous photograph. And allow me to add this as well: I said that in our report, collective report, we stated that most of the bodies wore dark clothes. However, we did not say that all of the persons had dark clothes on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I realise that, Professor Dobricanin. I'm going to discuss that with you a little later on. I'd like to move on to a discussion about a different person who died at Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I see those photographs, Mr. Prendergast, just for one moment. The other photographs of the bodies in the gully. Okay. If this photograph which is number 25 from the Finnish expert report could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see this photograph, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see that there is a body on the left-hand side marked Racak 33? Do you see that? You can only see a portion of the body. Is that a yes, Professor? Can you see that body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it, yes, in the upper-left corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. This is a man named Raif Salihu, who was unfortunately listed both by Judge Marinkovic and the Prosecution as Raif Jashari as well. And in Exhibit C1, page 11, again Dr. Ranta explains to the Trial Chamber that an examination of a bullet recovered from this body during the autopsy and bullet samples recovered in the gully in November of 1999 were fired from the same weapon. Again, those were bullets as I showed you on the previous photograph that were found in the ground beneath the position where these bodies were. Again, are you able to comment whether the information I've just given you might indicate that Mr. Raif Salihu was shot where he lay assuming that everything I've told you is true and correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that based on this photograph, especially where this body is concerned, nobody had a right to mark this body with RA33, because this is very unclear, and it is impossible to conduct a reconstruction based on the table -- on the bodies we had on the tables and the picture here on the site. Second, the Finnish team, Mrs. Ranta namely, complained that she was unable to get a single projectile or any other piece of material to take it with them to Finland because that was material subject to criminal technical investigation on our side, the organs in Pristina. Therefore, I don't know how come somebody came to take this projectile with them, how they managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry to cut you off. I said at the end of my question assuming everything I told you was correct: The position of the body, the position of the bullet or bullet fragments, the location of a bullet inside the body during an autopsy. Assuming all of that is correct, can we conclude that that person was shot where he lay, Mr. Salihu?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I challenge this photograph itself. It is very difficult for me to give approximate answers when I don't have the exact facts in front of me. Is it really this projectile? I don't know. For example, if we had two projectiles and had -- if we were able to compare them -- please allow me to conclude my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to answer. If these two projectiles were fired from the same weapon or if the projectile was taken out of the body and then fired from another identical weapon, and if you placed this under the microscope then we can establish with full certainty that these are projectiles fired from the same weapon. However, in this case, this is all not conclusive because we don't have any practical evidence showing that these bodies had not been moved, had not been manipulated with. And as you know, we did not have access to these bodies. Had we seen those bodies, we would have been able to tell you something different, perhaps something that would support what you're saying or support what I'm saying. You can tell me about what I saw there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, you say we have -- first of all, you're asking for practical evidence that the bodies have not been moved, which of course is asking to prove a negative. But secondly, we're showing you photographs of bodies at least where they were -- where they were seen on the 16th of January. We've discussed autopsy findings. We've discussed DNA analysis. We've discussed the findings of bullets in the soil beneath the position where the bodies were found on the 16th. How can you say that you have no practical information now to give an opinion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, how can you claim that the bodies were not moved? You know that we did not -- we were not present when the site was investigated. And who is it that conducted the investigation and videotaped the bodies without our presence? This is a sort of a violation of the established procedure. This means that they wanted to conceal something that we needed to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, when you say "they" wanted to conceal something, who is "they"? Just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the people who were present in Racak on the 15th, 16th, and the 17th of January, 1999. These are the people who banned us from accessing the area. And this ban entailed threats of Mr. John Drewienkiewicz and also the shooting that we encountered three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, if you were to assume that the bodies had not been moved, if you were asked to make an assumption, would you be able to answer Mr. Saxon's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, based on that assumption, I would not be able to give an answer. I'm a person who deals with facts. I am a factographer and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Speaking of facts, Professor Dobricanin, do you see that body in the photograph, RA21? Do you see that body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And he -- in the photograph, the body is wearing what appears to be some kind of a white jacket. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Prendergast, I'd like to ask for your assistance again. First, if we could show -- this is photographs taken when the autopsy was commenced of RA21 and the first piece of clothing that was removed. The ERN is 01089663. If that could be placed on the ELMO, followed by another photograph which is number 28 from the European Union report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, you see this photograph in front of you. Can we agree that this is a white jacket?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not a white jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, how would you describe this item in this photograph? How would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a grey colour. Let me just tell you this: Digital photography can change the appearance. It was white in the previous photograph and now it's grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the next photograph, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, we see the same bodies in this next photograph, the bodies lying in the gully. We can see body Racak 21 up in the top of the photograph, but lower down I want to show you something else. Do you see body Racak 32? He appears to be lying on his back or on his side. Do you see that photograph? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Take a look at the footwear that Racak 32 appears to be wearing. Do you see something red, appear to be either red boots or shoes or red socks? Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are most likely red boots with thick soles. Sir, please take a look at the next body to the left wearing military boots, number 70 -- 27F, on the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I wanted to show you another photograph, if I can. This is a photograph taken during the autopsy of body Racak 32, and these are his boots or whatever you want to -- however you choose to refer to his footwear. Can we agree, Dr. Dobricanin, that these appear to be red-coloured boots?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so. Dark red, at least based on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier in your testimony that the fact that some of the persons who died at Racak were dressed in dark clothing is an indicator that these persons were members of an armed group. Do you remember that testimony? Just do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, I've just shown you photographs which indicate that at least some of the people who died at Racak that day were wearing either light-coloured clothing or, as in the case of body number 32 found in the gully, rather bright-coloured clothing. Following your logic, Professor Dobricanin, can we assume that these persons who were wearing light-coloured clothing or bright-coloured clothing were civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you didn't follow closely what I said. I said that the vast majority. And this is something that could be seen on these photographs. However, you chose not to comment on that. We said that most of them wore dark clothing, that most of them had identical footwear on their feet which were boots with a zipper and mark or text Ozel. Most of the clothing on the victims in Racak were civilian clothes; however, of dark colour both for the top clothing and bottom clothing. Naturally, there were some people who did not have these shoes and who did not dark-coloured clothing, so they put on what they had. However, the vast majority had the dark-colour clothes. You are pulling out just one example out of a total number of example where the boots differ. These are warm winter boots, and I wore similar boots when it was very cold and when the snow was very deep, whenever I worked outside in the field in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, I'm pulling out individual examples because time prohibits me from reviewing every single body from Racak, but if as you testified last week dark clothing would be worn by a person in an armed unit who would have to spend a lot of time in the mountains, can't we conclude that a person who is wearing light-coloured clothing or bright-coloured clothing would not be a member of such a group, because it would be quite dangerous for that person would be wearing the clothing that they're wearing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They wore what they had. The tendency was to wear black or dark blue. There were also persons who in the summer months wore sports clothing, and they were members of the KLA. If they did not have such clothes, they wore what they had. And among themselves, knew each other. They recognised each other, and there was no need for them to wear clothes of special colour. Those who had such clothes wore them. Those who didn't wore what they had. However, in previous photographs we saw that people -- some people wore dark-coloured jeans or black jackets. However, the colour can be distorted and is distorted in some of the photographs. That is problem that you have with photography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, can I ask you? You said that some of them had boots with a zipper marked Ozel. Is there any significance to that marking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, sir, no. No, Your Honour Judge Robinson. It just means that they received from somebody a number of pairs of that footwear because they were unable to obtain military boots or something. As you were able to see, one in the persons in the photograph has military-style boots. Ozel I believe comes from Turkey. They received humanitarian aid, different kinds of goods from various sources probably including these boots. I did not claim that these were military boots. However, they did come from the same source. There were some people among them who wore military boots. What is important, though, is that those people wore the best kind of clothes they had for that season. They wore several layers of warm clothing, and they -- most of them attempted to have dark clothes in order to show their affiliation. This is what showed that they were affiliated with the village guards or Territorial Defence or whatever you want to call that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Roughly how many bodies had dark clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember that, Your Honour, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you say the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the majority. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few more questions related to gunpowder analysis, Professor Dobricanin. Yesterday, you explained in your testimony that when the bodies were brought to the morgue in Pristina and placed there, at some point after that first gunpowder analysis was performed on the hands of the bodies, and then subsequent to that fingerprint analysis was performed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the scientific reason for doing the gunpowder analysis first is because if the fingerprint analysis were done first that could contaminate the samples; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, there are some things that could be done to protect hands that need to be subjected to gunpowder analysis test, I believe, and -- for example, one option might be to try to protect the hands, placing paper bags over them; is that correct? I realise it was not done in this case, but I just need to confirm this with you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Another way of protecting the reliability or the validity of these scientific tests would be to do the test as soon as possible. For example, within several hours after the alleged use of a weapon. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as you explained, obviously in this case, given the circumstances, the gunpowder analysis was not done until several days after the incident in Racak; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not through any fault of ours, rather it was due to those people banned us from entering Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you a couple of orders, Professor Dobricanin. These are two orders issued by Judge Marinkovic on the 19th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There should be two. I gave you one this morning. Well, let's use the English. Is it possible, Ms. Dicklich, to get the other one? Now, if this could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 19th of January, Professor, and the Serbian version is there as well. I hope you can see it. First we have the English, then we have the Serbian version. It's from --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have my version in front of me. The English one is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. It's from Danica Marinkovic in relation to the autopsy of 40 corpses found in the mosque at the village of Racak, and it's an order to the -- it doesn't specifically say who it is to. It does at the bottom. It says, "Submitted to the forensic technician section in Pristina." And among other things, it orders the forensic technician section to perform the foil glove test on each body and to perform the fingerprint test. Do you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The foil glove test, that would be a reference to a testing for gunpowder analysis, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to be completely fair to the witness, Mr. Saxon says here, "Submitted to the forensic technician section in Pristina," which is true, but then below that it says also Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina. So I think he ought to quote it in its entirety, not just half of the sentence in order for the witness to be fully aware of the implications of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's the three letters ISM Pristina. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- can we conclude that this reference to the foil glove test is a reference to a gunpowder analysis test using some foil? Can we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are foil gloves which replace the test that was used previously using the paraffin and the gauze. So these are the glove foils which have five fingers from both sides, the upper and the bottom side, in order to detect all the particles and the location. This is the test that is used nowadays. They use the diphenylamine foils and the paraffin is out of use nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so this would have been the test pursuant to this -- pursuant to this order, then this kind of test would have been performed on the bodies from Racak; correct? Please just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show a bit of video, please. Before we start the video, we need to explain it. I've been in the evenings the last few nights going through video materials in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor trying to see if the Office of the Prosecution is in possession of video material that might show gunpowder analysis tests or other kinds of tests on the hands of these victims. And last night at about 6.00, I found some video that I'd like to show to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The quality of the photography is quite dark. The quality of the sound is less than perfect. But I'd like to show this to you, Professor Dobricanin, because you may be able to explain to us what is going on there. You may not be, but I'd like to show you a few minutes of this video and see if you can tell us what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we have sound if there is sound?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see bodies on the floor in the morgue. Body 17 on the left there. It looks like body 16 on the right. Here is some sound. This is body 17 again. Body 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop the tape there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, are you able to tell from what you've seen and heard what procedure was being performed in this video?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything, it's such poor quality. There are English words. I think there was some Albanian spoken. All I heard clearly at one point was that somebody said "Take some other gloves not to infect one body with the material from another." That's all I heard. Otherwise I really don't know what this was all about. But what I did notice is what I keep claiming: That all the bodies were in black clothing or dark clothing, all the ones you've shown now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We also see that the bodies were lying on the floor -- well, let me take one step backward. I heard in the sound the sound of what I can only describe as -- I don't know if it was paper crinkling or if it was tape being removed. Did you hear any such sound and could you comment on what that might have been?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't hear. There was such a lot of sound and noise that you couldn't differentiate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, you were there on the 20th? I might have heard your voice but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't at the autopsy in the morgue. I was in the hall where the autopsies take place. You couldn't have heard my voice. I would have recognised it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, the bodies were lying there on the floor. We could see blood spots on the floor. Is it possible that hands of victims could have been contaminated by contact with the floor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They weren't close together, and you -- hands wouldn't have been able to have been contaminated with gunpowder particles or nitrates from the blood spots on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could hands have been contaminated by other material on the floor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on that particular floor there was nothing else, and the floor was wiped every evening. It is washed with a hose every evening and then the bodies are brought into a clean area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Professor Dobricanin, that the bodies of at least 24 persons who were killed in Racak were tested for fingerprints while they still lay in the mosque on the 18th of January? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't see it in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if this could be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is in English and B/C/S, Serbian, so you can read the Serbian, Professor Dobricanin. It's a document again that I found last evening. I should say I found it last evening with the help of some of my colleagues. The first page has the case file of what I believe is the Serbian judicial system on it, case A/VI-025, and then it says "Enclosure, 2.13." And then it says fingerprint identification of 24 persons killed in Racak village... dated 29 January 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Ms. Dicklich, if we could distribute the aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the ELMO is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but may I correct you. It's the 29th of January, 1999, not the 21st. The 29th of January, 1999 is the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the first page, please. The first page says the first page at the top it says 269/99. It's from the Crime Investigation Department, Republic of Serbia, Secretariat in Pristina. Then it's titled "Dactyloscopic Identification of Dermal Ridge Print" and it explains how on 18 January 1999 forensic technician Sasa Bozanic conducted a forensic examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Saxon, do you have the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you should too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. All we have is the one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is the document I was referring to. I apologise for my confusion. And if that could be placed on the ELMO, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, the cover page shows the case file and the title, "Finger print [sic] identification of 24 persons." And then on the first page we see that it's from the Crime Investigation Department, Pristina. It's dated the 29th of January, 1999. "Dactyloscopic Identification of Dermal Ridge Print," and it describes how "On the 18th of January, 1999, Forensic Technician Sasa Bozanic... fixed impressions of dermal ridges for comparison with a right index finger print" to compare with the "personal identity card in the name of Mufailj Hajrizi," as one of the victims who died at Racak, victim Racak 03. Do you see this, Professor Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, just for the Trial Chamber's information, I have with me here the other 23 files. They are -- they are exactly the same with perhaps the differences of a comma here or a space here. They all say the same thing. And I'd rather use my time more efficiently at this point by simply showing one of them to the Trial Chamber. And the aide-memoire that I've also just given you gives -- provides the list of the names whose fingerprints were taken on the 18th in the mosque, their autopsy number, as well as the handwritten number which you can see on this page in the upper right-hand corner, A/VI-25/20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Professor Dobricanin, this report would seem to indicate that fingerprint test were is done on 24 of the victims two or three days before any gunpowder analysis tests were done, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't following you. Could you repeat your question, please? I was looking at these findings, and I'm not sure I followed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You have a file. It has the fingerprint identification reports of 24 persons killed in Racak, 24 of the persons who are listed in this indictment, and according to these reports, each report says that the fingerprint test was conducted in the mosque in Racak on the 18th of January, 1999. So my question is: That would indicate, wouldn't it, that fingerprint tests were conducted on 24 of the victims before any gunpowder analysis testing was done; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You did not understand it properly or perhaps it wasn't translated correctly. This first paragraph when it says on the 1th of January, 1999, the forensic technician, et cetera, et cetera, gives his findings and says, "On the basis of established principles and dactyloscopic identification -- dactyloscopic identification on at least 12 -- of at least 12 identical anatomic features/characteristics, it was established that the aforementioned impressions of dermal ridges are identical to the print of the right index finger of Mufailj Hajrizi, born..." et cetera, et cetera, "by dactyloscopy on 20 January 1999 at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina. Unidentified body labelled number RA03..." So it wasn't on the 18th of January that this was conducted, it was when they were found in the mosque. Whereas the dactyloscopy took place on the 20th of January, 1999 at the Institute for Forensic Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin, if dermal ridges were placed on the hands on the 18th of January, that is done as part of a test for fingerprints, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not conducted on the 18th of January. That was done on the 20th of January and wasn't done at the mosque but at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina. Take a look at the last paragraph where it says that under "Findings." Look at "Findings," that last paragraph, and you'll see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this refers to -- this is the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And the preamble says, Professor Dobricanin, that "On 18 January... Technician Sasa Bozanic fixed impressions of dermal ridges" for comparisons with the fingers of this man, Mufailj Hajrizi." So that would mean that something was done on the hand of this man on the 18th of January, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the mosque in Racak and nobody conducted any dactyloscopy under the conditions that prevailed when they started firing with mortars. What I tell you is certain: All traces of dermal ridge for dactyloscopy, all gunpowder findings, all samples were taken at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina. Before that nothing had been done with respect to the crime and technical research except for the photographs. The photographs were taken in the mosque in the village of Racak. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, why did Sasa Bozanic record having performed this work on the 18th of January? Why did he go to all this trouble?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there two procedures, two stages, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or the Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. This is probably an error in the preamble because he refers to the date when we took over the corpses. But it says quite clearly when all the prints were taken, and that took place on the 20th of January whereas -- at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina. That's what it says. And I state to Your Honour Judge Robinson that nothing was done in Racak. I say that quite clearly and unequivocally because there were no conditions for anything to be done or conducted. It is no place in which you would take samples for dactyloscopy. So the only correct thing is this: It is the findings which clearly state what was done and where and when.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I be of assistance to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have here in the Serbian original is a form, a form. It's not that Bozanic said "fixed impressions of dermal ridges." It is a pre-printed form for dactyloscopic identification of dermal ridge print and he was just filling in the form, whereas the findings tell us what the professor has been saying, when the dactyloscopy was performed. So this is -- whereas this is a form, a general form, a printed form and you just fill in the empty spaces. And if you look at the original you'll see this very easily. You'll see what the form contains, the pre-printed form, and what they filled in. So the sections filled in coincide exactly with what the professor was telling us, whereas how -- what the pre-printed form is quite unimportant for this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I tell you something else and to indicate a portion of this document? Might I be allowed to do that? On the last page, which is where you will see the fingerprints themselves, here I have it. You can look at this on my copy. It's the last page showing the fingerprints themselves, it says the following: Family name and first name and other particulars; and then it says date of registration and the date there is the 20th of January, 1999. That clearly indicates that it was on that day that the fingerprints were taken from this individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why was the 18th filled in? Why did they fill in the 18th at the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a printed form, and it says "on the 18th," et cetera, et cetera. It's probably a mistake. When you fill in forms, you don't -- they do it very often mechanically and fill in the blanks that way, mechanically. So maybe that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two blanks show different dates. I mean, could you possibly explain why the 18th would be put in there at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the date when the bodies were taken over from the mosque. So that was the date recorded, because that was the first time we came into contact with the bodies, and then he couldn't say that they were from the bodies from the 15th in Racak. We never recorded that way when you give a crime -- to the crime technician. This was the date, and he clearly said that the technical part of the business was done on the 20th of January, 1999, at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina, and you'll see the fingerprints on the last page where the date is the 20th of January, 1999, again, and it's written in in handwriting. It's fairly small but you can see it, where it says date, registration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document I would like to show, two documents, actually. One of them is a request for assistance from the Office of the Prosecution to the government of Serbia from 2002, I believe in May, and the second document is a response from the government of Serbia from the summer of 2002. I'll pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, Judge Kwon reminds me that we are dealing with the exhibits individually. So those that are -- that can be admitted, which are not going to be controversial, we should admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, would I offer for admission the documents that I have just provided to the Trial Chamber regarding the fingerprint analysis, and then we will very briefly discuss these two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think there were some before that, so maybe we had better deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, the letter of -- the request for assistance from May 2002 asked the government of Serbia questions regarding gunpowder analysis testing that were done on the bodies in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- can that be placed on the ELMO, please? And can it be moved up a little bit, please. Can it be moved up a little bit more. And the next page, please. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's a question there -- there are two questions. It says "If the test was positive, what further tests were applied on that person?" And then it asks: "What tests were carried out to establish the source of contamination?" In other words, the source of an indication of nitrates. Actually, this is the response, which is perfectly fine. It makes life simpler. And the response of the government of Serbia that we're looking at here underneath the question says that: "In the concrete situation (Racak), there were no conditions to check whether there was any contamination in the case of persons for whom the above test was positive, that is, there were no realistic conditions to try to establish contamination sources." Professor Dobricanin, is that a fair statement do you think?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a true statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would offer these two documents for admission as well, Your Honour, at the appropriate time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to go back just very briefly, Professor Dobricanin, to the subject of colours of clothing, because you made a comment that I wanted to discuss with you. You said "they wore whatever they had." That was earlier this morning, I think in response to a question from Judge Robinson. What would people who were not members of a KLA or a village defence force wear?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the people in the village were uniformed. You know that there are different types of clothing. But these tried to have the black colour prevail which showed their affiliation to a village guard or a terrorist organisation or the special police, and their colour was exclusively black.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not sure if you understood my question. It was very different. My question was: What would people who were not members of a KLA unit or a village defence force wear?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't know. Well, if you don't know, then how could we ever know -- if -- if there's no correlation between clothing worn by a person and the possibility that that person could be a civilian or not, then why is there a correlation between colour of clothing worn by a person and the possibility that that person is a member of an armed unit? I don't understand how you can say one thing and not the other.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that you understood what I was saying. I said that the members of those military organisations wore predominantly black clothing or almost every time black clothing, especially their special police, whereas the other farmers and peasants that didn't belong to them - not everybody was a member of the KLA - it would be something else, then. They wore the clothing they had. The members of the KLA wore exclusively black, black-coloured clothing or dark clothing if they didn't have parts of a black uniform. They didn't actually have uniforms. They did what they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, so I think, then, by that logic if a policeman entered Racak on the 15th of January and saw a person wearing light clothing, that person would -- that policeman would not know whether the person wearing the light clothing was a civilian or a member of an armed unit, would he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no answer to that question. It's hypothetical, an assumption. I can't think along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, the problem that we have here is that we have a number of bodies in the gully and in other areas around Racak, people shot from all different directions, bullets found in different parts of their bodies. We have people wearing dark-coloured clothing but also people wearing light-coloured clothing. We have people wearing several layers of clothing, but it was wintertime. We have -- apparently gunpowder analysis was done but we have no formal results of that analysis. We certainly have indications that the analysis was not carried out under optimal conditions. We have forensic examinations done by the European Union team that places bullets underneath bodies where they were found, as well as parts of bodies, and we have no information that weapons were found next to anyone that was killed in Racak. So can't we simply conclude that all of these persons were killed where they were found and that they were unarmed? Isn't that a possible conclusion for the events in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you listened to me carefully over the past few days, I made four assumptions. I focused on four points, and I gave very precise answers to those questions both to the Trial Chamber and to you yourself. You have now made a compilation of all this, and I just can't answer that. I can only take them one by one. Your conclusion is your own conclusion. It is not my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. And your conclusions are based on your four assumptions. Isn't that right, Professor Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And my conclusions are based on these assumptions, and they do not speak of unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes. Mr. Saxon, when we return, we will deal with those exhibits that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With your leave, I would ask permission to ask one or two more questions. It's because I realised during the break at the last session I made a comment that was not completely fair to the witness and I should have asked him a question about a topic before making my comment. So with your leave, I'd like to ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, going back to the analysis of the hands of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the bodies for gunpowder residue, the -- and you have testified that 37 out of 40 bodies tested tested positive for nitrates. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why weren't these results recorded in your autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one single reason. We expected all the results of the ridge prints and the identification and everything. I didn't even have a list of the killed persons. We expected all the results of the gunpowder analysis to come as return information, that one copy should go to the investigating judge and that we should get yet another copy for our own documentation. The only reason why this did not happen is, I think, the fact that all the people working on this were very busy, extremely busy. We had a very difficult situation over those several months, and because this was prepared together with the video footage and the photographs that was all supposed to be handed over to us. All of this was destroyed, however, during the bombing of the SUP. So there is no other reason but that for the fact that we haven't got all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that you were -- you were too busy to record these results on the autopsy results, that time did not allow it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In our notes, in the records that we had that remained at the Institute, we certainly recorded that there was a positive reaction as far as nitrates are concerned. We just gave the figure of 37 positive for nitrates. We thought that there was no reason to publish this in detail. You saw the Finnish reports too. They did not describe all of these findings in detail. This wasn't enough material in all cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say "there wasn't enough material in all cases too." Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that since the so-called paraffin glove was already taken, that is to say this foil glove that the technicians used, that there was a little bit of that material on the hands and that that is probably why my colleagues from Finland did not pursue this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Very briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: More than a little bit, not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall telling investigator Barney Kelly that you did not record your findings regarding gunpowder residue because there wasn't sufficient time to do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. This is a different question. He's now asking whether you remember telling the investigator Barney Kelly that you didn't record your findings relating to gunpowder residue because there wasn't enough time to do that. This is a different question, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, this was recorded in the collective findings of the group of forensic pathologists from Serbia and the forensic pathologists in Belorussia -- in Belarus. I haven't got the findings here. It was stated that in 37 cases traces were found of nitrate on the hands. That was our collective finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you have an interview with Barney Kelly, the investigator Barney Kelly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, for two days in Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What Mr. Saxon is calling -- is asking is if you remember telling him at that you didn't record the findings relating to gunpowder residue because there wasn't enough time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. I told him what I am saying here today, that we did not get these findings. We did not receive them because there wasn't time for that. But we did record the findings in our general conclusions. The results regarding gunpowder particles and nitrates have been recorded in one sentence, as I said a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, I'd like to exhibit the prior statement of Professor Dobricanin. I will do this as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I would invite the parties to turn to page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin, I don't have a Serbian translation, but I will read you the appropriate passages so that you can -- you can hear the translation in your language. First of all, take a look at the top page. Do you see your name written there, Slavisa Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you see how on every page your signature is at the bottom? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at page 12, please, the English version. At the very top of the page it says: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language, and I have been invited to make any alterations or additions that I deem necessary, but I do not wish to do so. This statement is correct." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you look at page 9, please. And in the fourth paragraph on page 9, you describe the gunpowder analysis tests that were done, and in the second to the last sentence you say: "These important findings were not added to our written conclusions because we did not have time." Do you recall saying that to Investigator Kelly now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've said that, but I've explained to you just now why it was put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him give the explanation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain again, because I'm not -- at least I'm not following your explanation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when an autopsy is done, the forensic pathologist does the autopsy. Crime technicians take samples of whatever is necessary from the hands and finally on the spot. These are biological traces, traces of explosion, et cetera, and we did that on all the bodies from Racak. They took these samples of theirs to the crime technical laboratory of the provincial SUP in Pristina. We received information about all the cases with numbers and with positive analyses. We recorded these analyses in our working notebooks which we took when we went to autopsy the 40 bodies. In the collective report that was written on the 30th of January, 1999, on the basis of this information we wrote that on 37 bodies, on the hands of 37 bodies, traces were found of nitrates, which may indicate that there were particles of gunpowder too. In view of the format of the general report, we believed that that was quite sufficient. We expected in the following months that when all of this was processed, we would get photographs, video footage, and analyses of the crime technical services related to gunpowder particles and the names of persons who were killed in the village of Racak. All of that was being prepared, and I said that on Thursday or Friday that there were about 18.000 photographs, a couple of hundred video recordings, video cassettes, and other documentation, which after everything that happened, was supposed to be handed over to the Institute and the investigating judge Mrs. Danica Marinkovic. Since all of this was on the premises of the crime technical service of the provincial SUP all of this was destroyed during the bombing of the SUP. So would did not get a single shred of information about all these documents. Actually we did not receive a single document. The only written trace that remained is our general conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic. I'm sorry. Mr. Saxon, those exhibits that can be admitted should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would start with the statement of Professor Dobricanin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then starting chronologically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement of Dobricanin would be 848.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The ICTY witness statement of Rizah Salihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'd like to hear whether there's any objection from the accused. I don't expect him to oppose to this but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The statement that deals with the name of the dead person. Did you say no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections, but I'm going to put a question. The name of Raif Salihu was mentioned here. Raif Salihu or Jashari. The question is whether it's Salihu or Jashari. Is not on the list contained in Schedule A, neither as Salihu or as Jashari. So from that point of view, this statement does not match the information contained in here. Since Mr. Saxon explained that it was possible that Salihu is the same as Jashari. However, Raif is not in Schedule A either as Salihu or Jashari. So that is what I wanted to ask about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he is in Schedule A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: He very clearly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Jashari Raif, 20 years of age." Okay. There's no objection from the accused on this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then there were 3 photographs, the photo of the grave of Jashar Salihu, Raif Salihu, and Shukri Salihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was the ICTY statement of Milazim Syla or Syla, depending on your language, dealing with victim Sabri Syla on Judge Marinkovic's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There were three photographs from the Racak cemetery, the grave of Arif Metushi, Sabri Metushi and Haki Metushi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was a chart or an aide-memoire dealing with the names of the persons killed at Racak on the 15th of January and a compilation of information available about those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation from assigned counsel or the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit? Was this meant to be exhibited or just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour, for your assistance. For the assistance of everyone, quite frankly, because the issue of names is confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then we have an order signed by Danica Marinkovic dated the 19th of January, 1999, regarding autopsies and other processes concerning the 40 bodies taken from Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I suppose I should go in a more logical order. The sample from what's called the enclosure 2.13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fingerprints.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Finger print identification of 24 persons killed in the Racak village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering all of them or one of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Unless the Trial Chamber feels it's necessary, again to cut down on paper to be more efficient, we would simply tender one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to hear from the Defence, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anything on this, Mr. Kay or Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then the final item would simply be another aide-memoire simply listing for you the persons who are named in that file as having had the fingerprint work done starting on the 18th of January. There are 24 of them, so it does not -- it does not refer to every victim. Twenty-four of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that is all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. There are correspondences between ICTY and Mr. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am grateful to Your Honour for being sharper than I am this morning. We had a request for assistance from May 2002 from the ICTY to the government of Serbia. Sorry, it would be one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we had a respond from the government of Serbia in the summer of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Dobricanin, please take a look at this document that was exhibited a few moments ago by Mr. Saxon. This is the respond of the Federal Ministry of Justice to the questions put in relation to the paraffin test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What exhibit was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 858. Will the Registrar see that the witness has the correct document. Yes. Do you have the document, Professor? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, Mr. Saxon only pointed to one of the answer that I will deal with, but before that I would like to check a few other things. On page 1 of this of this response, in response to the third question, "What level of training was required from persons conducting the test," the answer is "the collection of gunpowder particles may only be done by forensic technicians who finished a course for forensic technicians, where they were specially trained. "Only adequately qualified experts (physico-chemists, chemists, technologists...) who completed internal specialist training may check for gunpowder particles by applying the diphenylamine test." Are you aware of this, and was a standing practice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by experts in chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The last question was what kind of quality control was performed, and the answer is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry but they cannot find the reference that is being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the terms -- that's on page 2, the one, two, three, fourth question on page 2 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that customary procedure, and is this correct what it says here, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is the customary procedure of testing solutions. This is what our technicians do. And we have that which we got precisely for these purposes, and we used to conduct this on our own too. And this is done before every procedure for testing nitrates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Please look at the next two questions and answers. Could you just comment on that? The question here is: "What is the total number of tests conducted in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?" With this paraffin glove, if I can call it that. And it says here -- let me just read the answer. And I assume that it is also correct, but I want you to compare it. "It is not possible to give a precise answer because the whole documentation was burned in the bombing of the Secretariat of the Interior building in Pristina. It is estimated that diphenylamine tests were carried out in over 2.000 cases." So in your opinion, is this estimate also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a correct estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. That will do. Thank you. The next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was -- just before this continues, have I wrongly understood that in fact the paraffin test was not the one used here, that the test used was a different one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Bonomy, I think that perhaps you misunderstood it. It is called the paraffin test. It is called the paraffin test because earlier, previously, the particles were taken off, were lifted with a melted paraffin. At that time it was called the paraffin test. Nowadays we call it both paraffin test and adhesive foil test. But nowadays we use diphenylamine with a certain acid. So these are two identical tests with two different names. It used to be known as the paraffin test but nowadays paraffin is not used any more because paraffin does not participate at all in the reaction needed in order to carry out this test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is actually describing the test which was carried out in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Professor, based on your -- what you know, this statement in this letter of the Ministry of Justice to the effect that this was carried out in over 2.000 cases coincides with your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next question is how many of these tests were positive, and the replay states: "It is not able to give an answer for the above-mentioned reasons. It is estimated that the result was positive in about 50 per cent of the cases." Professor, does that mean that in those cases where it was suspected that weapons were used and where paraffin test was conducted, in 50 per cent of those cases roughly it turned out that the result was positive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. In 50 per cent of the cases or perhaps a bit less, it is probable that people did not use weapons, and this is why we obtained 50 per cent negative reactions to nitrates. And in cases where there were nitrate traces on the hands, the results were 50 per cent. However, this is a rough estimate. I don't think that this is entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, all right. I understand you. If I understood you well, when it is believed that a person fired from a weapon, from a firearm, then the paraffin test is applied. And based on what is stated in the answer, in 50 per cent of the cases the suspicion proved to be right, that in 50 per cent of the cases the person did fire from a firearm whereas in 50 per cent of the cases the person did not, and the test was not positive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
