utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this particular case in Racak we have this figure 50 per cent. In view of the fact that you tested or, rather, that this test was used in all 40 cases, meaning hundred per cent of the persons that you examined, and the positive result was obtained in 37 of the cases, this means that in this particular case the positive result was obtained in 92.5 per cent of the samples, tested bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, last week, based on your experience in the use of this test, you said -- I'm not going to quote verbatim what you said, but you said something along the lines that based on your experience, in almost all of the cases where the test was positive, later on in the investigation it was confirmed via other tests used or via other analyses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just -- my objection is simply that the -- I think it's important that the -- if the accused is going to cite from the record that he needs to do it accurately. And my recollection of the testimony of this witness is that he was not aware of cases that tested positive which then turned out to be wrong or incorrect. However, at no time did he say what he based his -- his findings on, whether additional tests had been made or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't have the record in front of me, but do I have a recollection of testimony in that direction. Mr. Milosevic, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Professor to confirm the following: We had this general situation concerning the application of the paraffin test based on the answers given by the Ministry of Justice where it says that in 50 per cent of the cases it was confirmed that nitrates were present. And here in Racak the percentage was 92.5 per cent. So that was the percentage of cases where the test was positive. I asked Professor to confirm or deny that, and he confirmed it. The next question says as follows: "Were the tests carried out in accordance with international standards, and if yes, what standards were these?" And then it says that the test was applied in accord and with the criteria described in all forensic textbooks in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Professor, based on your experience, not only in Yugoslavia but also based on your professional contacts with experts from other countries, do you claim that this test is always conducted in the same way in accordance with the standards found in forensic textbooks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The following question: "Were the tests on the dead people from Racak consistent with other tests which were carried out at the time?" The answer was yes. "Were the dead persons tested in the same way as live ones?" "Yes." So therefore there is no difference here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they go on to say precisely how many persons were qualified to carry out the paraffin test in the SFRY in 1998 and 1999 and how many of such persons lived in Kosovo and in the area. The answer was 35, 35 forensic technicians and one permanent expert who was in the Secretariat of the Interior in Pristina. Therefore, was this number of staff sufficient in order to carry out reliable tests which would be in accordance with forensic textbooks and which would be needed in order to apply the test properly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite a sufficient number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, I would like to go back to another question now highlighted by Mr. Saxon, which can be found on page 1, and that is what kind of tests was conducted in order to establish the source of contamination? And then this says that in Racak, in the concrete situation in Racak there were no conditions to check, whether there was any contamination in the case of persons for whom the above test was positive. That is, there were no realistic conditions to try to establish contamination sources. And you said that this was stated correctly. And you basically confirmed everything else in this document. So this claim, does it challenge at all the conclusions reached by the paraffin tests?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's quite enough for this document. Now I would like you to take a look at the document that you already commented upon, also the document offered into evidence by Mr. Saxon, which is an example out of this binder for Racak, which is the dactyloscopic identification of ridge lines. I hope that you have that before you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please tell us, is this a form, a pre-printed form that has been printed in advance and contains certain blanks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it has been copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the criminal technician filling in the blanks will basically take this form, pre-printed form, and simply fill in data pertaining to the particular case that he's investigating.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What created confusion here is that in the beginning, it states the 18th of January, and I would like to ask you the following: Since it says here "On the," and then blank and he typed in the 18th of January, and then it says, "Forensic Technician," and then blank and he inserted his name, Sasa Bozanic. And it says, "Conducted a forensic examination of an incident scene following the discovery of 40 unidentified bodies in Racak." Is it clear, based on this document, that the 18th of January Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pertains to the date when the bodies were found in Racak in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection. Is it clear, Your Honour? It sounds a bit leading to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we've been through this several times. Questions beginning is it clear, et cetera, are usually leading questions. But I wonder why you're bothering with this, because I thought an explanation was given which was quite satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask one question about this. Do you know the technician Sasa Bozanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I remember the name but not the face. I knew some of the technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he at the mosque in Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is stated in this document, let us make it as brief as possible. We also have the enclosure with fingerprints and the dates and so on. Is it unequivocal as to the date when the fingerprinting was carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again, "Is it unequivocal," that's suggesting the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, based on this document, can one establish for a fact exactly when the fingerprinting was carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that stated in the form, and is it also stated on the fiche with fingerprints?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both documents, in both places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it then, Professor, you claim that Mr. Bozanic says he was doing on the 18th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just a major misunderstanding. When he was filling out the text, he probably wasn't reading the form. He simply inserted his name and the date when the bodies were found in Racak. I'm tell the truth. Mr. Sasa Bozanic was not present in Racak, and no fingerprints were taken in Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Dobricanin, are you able to answer the question who wrote this document? Is it Mr. Bozanic or Perunovic and Cirkovic who appear at the bottom of the document? According to the document, it seems to me that it was Bozanic that fixed an impression of dermal ridges, and those two people, there is a Perunovic and Cirkovic, made the findings on 20th of January. Could you assist me on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Bozanic took the fingerprints, lifted them off the bodies, and the other two, Zoran Perunovic is a chemical expert. The other two performed the analysis. These are people trained to conduct dactyloscopy and they carried out the identification of this person based on the previous information that existed in the SUP, the card that existed there, plus using the results obtained by dactyloscopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is those two chemical experts who wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not chemists. Not chemists. Persons trained to perform dactyloscopy and identification. I made a mistake. The chemical experts did another analysis which is the paraffin test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this Perunovic and Cirkovic wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They filled in and wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are those the persons who are supposed to carry out the identification?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are experienced crime technicians. Zoran Perunovic has a bachelor of science degree, and they were the ones who mostly worked on identification of dermal ridge prints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is stated here in the findings signed by them, that the dactyloscopy was carried out on the 20th of January, 1999 and that this is based on this card where by hand certain information is filled in, Racak, name, last name, and it says the date of registration the 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was filled in by Sasa Bozanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he filled in this form on the date when he took fingerprints, and then he spent it to them in order to carry out the identification. Was that the procedure carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can some foundation be laid as to how this witness knows that Sasa Bozanic filled in the form showing the fingerprints and dated the 20th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is actually a typewritten form, it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would appear that, Your Honour. But the date -- it's a typewritten form although the date appears obviously written in hand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Saxon please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a typewritten form but the date was written by someone in hand but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's typed in on the one I have. Do you have one that shows it handwritten? Everything's typed in, except the signatures of the two examining -- the fingerprint experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's looking at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm looking at the fingerprints themselves, Your Honour. You see a typewritten form, and the fifth line down we see the date written by someone's hand. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was referring to this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I have a doubt whether Mr. Bozanic typed this in himself, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since you haven't got the translation that is written in hand, it's a typewritten one, could replace the form on the overhead projector so we could have a look at what it actually looks like with the ten fingerprints. All the data there has been introduced by hand, all handwritten entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just so we can see it. All ten fingers, please. Just to have a look at the original. Is that what you see on the overhead projector, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as we can see, all these columns have been filled in by hand, the name the surname, the registration number, the date of registration, which is the 20th of January, 1999. The 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have a number under the right index finger. Does that mean that it was the only fingerprint that was on the ID card and on the basis of that they were able to establish, on the basis of that one fingerprint, who the person was, the identification?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the order issued by Judge Danica Marinkovic, which Mr. Saxon tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one thing before you move on. Mr. Saxon, does the date the 18th appear on all of these 24 forms?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Every single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as soon as I don't have all the 24 forms myself, I should like to ask the witness to take a look and see whether the date when the prints were taken in all 24 forms, does it appear as being the 20th of January as well, or does the 18th figure anywhere? Because it's quite clear what we're dealing with. It was the 18th when the bodies were found, and the 20th is the other date if the same dates appear in all 24 forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Body number 4, Ljutfi Biljali, the date on the form is 20 January. The date on the fingerprint form in the original is 20 January. 18th of January on the first form regarding the work of Sasa Bozanic. Body Racak number 5 belonging to Murtez Imeri, the -- on the fingerprints themselves it's handwritten 20 January, 1999, 18th of January on the first page dealing with the work of Sasa Bozanic in the mosque. Body Racak number 1, Banush Kameri, who is also Banush Azem. We see the form looks a little bit different, and I am frankly struggling to see a date here on this particular form. I don't know if the witness would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They should be passed to the witness. As you look at them, just pass them over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall we pass them to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, those three you've looked at already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I've lost my paper clip but I'll keep this in order. There is one more here. This one here, I am not finding any date on the particular fingerprint form. The work of Mr. Bozanic on the first page 18th of January, and then it says below, "examined by dactyloscopy examined on the 20th of January." Do you wish me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's going to be a laborious exercise, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's proceed this way: Mr. Saxon, continue looking at them, and then we can return to this later, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not now. Not now. Mr. Milosevic will continue with his re-examination, and we'll return to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can simply point out for everyone's information, I just happened to see one fingerprint form where there appears to be no date written on it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it does have the 20th at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the first form it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you could update the aide-memoire during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As I'm in my aide-memoire period, it seems, I will try to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That might be useful. So we'll come back to this, Mr. Milosevic. We haven't forgotten it, but let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, now, with respect to the order issued by Judge Danica Marinkovic, which states and I hope you have it before you: "I order that in cooperation with the forensic experts you should perform the following: Take the foil from every individual; obtain gunpowder analysis to establish the identity of the bodies; photograph -- photograph and to record on VHS tape each body separately and let that be submitted to the Court; to perform the expertise of each missile and foreign bodies found on the body to establish what kind of missile and weapon it's about."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says, "As well as to undertake all other necessary works at your discretion, if it deems necessary during the performance of above-mentioned works, tasks." Professor Dobricanin, this order by Judge Marinkovic, does it contain all the elements necessary, everything that is needed to be done in a procedure of this kind, and is it the customary, is it the usual way of issuing orders by a judge as to what should be done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this order, does it imply in that last line, that last point when it says "As well as to undertake all other necessary measures at your discretion if you deem necessary," et cetera, et cetera, for the previous things to be conducted, that covers everything, that nothing must be omitted [Realtime transcript read in error: "admitted"] which could be considered important for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very well-worded order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where it says that it should be submitted to Forensic technician section Pristina and ISM Pristina, does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting the accused but I think I've just seen an error in the transcript and I think simply the error needs to be clear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's what I thought was the error. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This order, then, is addressed to the police crime technical section, and the ISM is the Institute of Forensic Medicine of Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kwon asked you a question -- or, rather, asked Mr. Saxon a question with respect to the photographs that Mr. Saxon showed. Now, were those the photographs taken on the 15th and 16th of January? Mr. Saxon's answer was yes. Since I'm not aware of anybody taking any photographs on the 15th of January or, rather, as far as I know the photographs were made by the team with Walker only on the 16th of January, do you happen to know, are you aware of anybody taking photographs on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say you don't know that any photographs were taken on the 15th of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The photographs that were taken on the 16th of January were shown to you here in court. Now, do you know that the investigating judge, Mrs. Danica Marinkovic, had already on the 15th of January arrived at Racak but was then sent away by gunfire and was not able to carry out an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it incontestable, then, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, "Is it clear," "is it unequivocal," is it uncontestable" are leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, do you -- were you aware that Danica Marinkovic was in Racak on the 15th of January but had to leave because of the fire that she was exposed to along with her team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you also know that on the 16th of January, precisely at the time when Walker was in Racak, she attempted to reach Racak herself and that she was prevented in doing so by gunfire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you on the 17th of January, when you joined Danica Marinkovic, also attempt to reach Racak, to enter Racak together with the other members of the team but -- and you were very close to Racak, could see the village from a distance, but that you were once again prevented from entering because of firing and had to go back to return? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of January when you finally reached Racak and -- were you shot at?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic testified here and said that on the 15th, she saw weapons in Racak that had remained. You were shown weapons by the police. You saw trenches in Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw bunkers in Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, had knowledge and awareness of the fact that there was shooting in Racak on the 15th --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- well, he has already given that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, as for the most part attempts are made here to explain that this was killing and not a conflict, these are facts which had to be well known to one and all, and now I'm asking the witness this. I'm asking him whether it was, therefore, common knowledge that there was shooting in Racak both on the 15th and on the 16th and on the 17th and indeed on the 18th, all four days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you -- do you assume that some unarmed civilians did all the shooting during those days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's quite clear that somebody who was in the village and armed was doing the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You performed the paraffin test which showed that on 37 bodies that they had used arm -- firearms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, it's simply just to keep the record clear. The question was put with the pronoun "you." And I think it's simply quite clear that Professor Dobricanin has been clear that he personally did not perform these tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't that so, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not being challenged, Mr. Robinson, at all. When I say you, I don't mean him personally. I mean the experts who performed the task, and the Professor confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since it was common knowledge that there were trenches and bunkers and firing in those days at Racak, did any forensic expert -- were they able to say -- to write the sentence that I'm going to quote in his report, like the sentence in Mrs. Ranta's report where it says there were no indications of this involving people who would be anything else but unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they don't have the actual wording of that sentence before them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a matter which we will determine ultimately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, in tab 11, which was sent to the journalists on the 17th of March, 1999, it is almost -- not almost but in fact it's two months, 15th of January, 17th of March, and two days after the event, post festum. Did the Finnish team with Mrs. Ranta have any knowledge about the fact that the so-called paraffin test had been performed which she, on page 5, comments and says that it is not reliable?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We informed them about that when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd ever January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. The 22nd of January is when they arrived and when they were informed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 17th of March it is claimed that there were no indications which would confirm -- her sentence is a little unwieldy. She didn't say that they were unarmed citizens, she said there were no indications that this was a case of people who were anything else but unarmed civilians. That's the way she puts it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the subject we contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you say something -- could that kind of thing be said from a professional aspect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't see how the witness can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness is a forensic expert. He bears in mind all the indications, because indications are mentioned here. There are no indications. As a forensic expert himself, he can answer the question of whether we can -- one could say there were no indications. If he testifies that there were indeed indications and many indications at that, so that this is completely conflicting with the available facts, an assertion of this kind, saying that there were no indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You could ask him --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness claims there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You could ask him what indications there were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness claims there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That there were unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before we hear the witnesses answer, I think it also would be helpful to let the witness clarify whether he is answering in his capacity as an expert in forensic medicine or in his capacity as a citizen when he is referring to indications or assumptions, because throughout his testimony since last week he has told us that on certain matters he's testifying as an expert and in other matters he's speaking as a common citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what arises from the answer that he gives?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One thing that arises would be the amount of weight that the Chamber gives to his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But isn't that a matter that we'll have to determine?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, but you -- I don't see how the Trial Chamber will be in a position to determine it unless the witness clearly says that he is providing an answer in this case as an expert or in his capacity as a human being, or as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. Saxon, I find that a very tedious way to go about the work. I think we'll have to make up our minds when he's testifying as an expert. We have said -- we said at the very beginning that if you were prejudiced in any way by the lateness of the notification in relation to his evidence as an expert that we would allow you to make an application. We'll have to decide what evidence comes in from this witness as an expert and what is otherwise. I don't see that it is helpful to ask the witness in relation to every answer that he gives whether he's testifying as an expert or not. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, I'm going to follow Mr. Robinson's suggestion. He suggested that I ask you whether there were any indications. Now, before I put that question to you, please bear in mind that I'm asking you as a forensic expert. So in relation to this sentence, there were no indications that these were persons who would be anything but unarmed civilians. Professor, were there any indication that is these were not unarmed civilians but persons who were armed and who were shooting? Were there any indications and, if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to single out only two out of all the indicators. I've already spoken about this over the pass few days. First of all, it is not customary ever in the street when all of this was going on, and that is the early morning hours, to have so many people in the street wearing several layers of clothing. When I say that, I'm saying that this was truly clothing that was prepared for a longer stay outdoors. Secondly, the traces of nitrate on their hands which indicate but not with any certainty that firearms were used and also the distribution pattern of the traces indicates that they were armed and that they were shooting from firearms. These are two indicators which guide me as a forensic medical expert to believe that there was a struggle between the police and these people who were firing in Racak or, rather, that they were firing, that they were shooting. Were they were shooting, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Mr. Saxon gave some information here about casings and bullets found in November 1999 in Racak. You recall this information that he presented here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, Professor, on the basis of the fact that in November 1999, that is to say ten months after the event concerned, some bullets were found, casings on one side and bullets on the other. I don't want to waste any time to look for the sketch that Mr. Saxon showed you. Can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this lead to the conclusion that some kind of execution had taken place there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we were just to assume that on the location that was marked there casings were found and that bullets were really found in the place that was marked as such, the exit/entry wounds and their bullet-path directions, could they confirm that it was execution that took place from the place where the casings were to the place where the persons were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained today that the sketch leads me to believe that the bullet direction would be in -- on one level or they would move from forward to the back or from the back to the front, but certainly not from the top to the bottom, because the alleged pattern of the bodies indicates only this possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even if the facts were correct in relation to the location of the casings and the location of the bullets, that would not match the directions from which the firing came; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's another leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's leading, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked the professor whether I understood him correctly. If we have this assumption, if it would be correct where the bullets were and where the casings were, would it be possible to have these several directions of the exit/entry lines?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be no comparison. These bullet-path directions that we found during the autopsy would not fit into the sketch I saw today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- why did you not say that earlier when you were asked about it by Mr. Saxon if it's today's sketch that you're talking about, not the one that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did say it today. Precisely when Mr. Saxon was putting his questions to me. I said that the possible bullet-path directions are only possible on a particular plane that we are talking about and that it is impossible to have the paths going from the top to the bottom, to the left to the right if we look at the position of the bodies and the position of the pile of casings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, to the best of my recollection I did not show this witness any sketches of the bullet paths this morning. Yesterday I did. Today I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I'm not sure whether that particular question was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was put, Your Honour, in this particular context: The question roughly was, assuming the facts were correct, that a bullet was found in this position in the soil underneath a position where this particular body was found, could one draw a conclusion that the person was shot where they lay. That's how I put the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is about the bullet path. It's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At no point in the response was it about bullet paths, Your Honour, that I can recall. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why I say that particular question was not put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What concerns me is as far as today's evidence is concerned - I'm ignoring for the moment yesterday's - as far as today's evidence is concerned, the witness throughout his evidence has said, "I can draw no conclusions one way or another from paper, from what is presented to me on paper." And I'm concerned now that he is trying to draw conclusions from what is presented to him on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the transcript needs to be looked at because there was a look at the sketches of the bullet marks on two of the victims in the ravine, and the witness made a comment about the angle of the marks on the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It seems that we haven't clarified this sufficiently. So let us proceed with the assumption presented by Mr. Saxon. Did you understand that the place where the casings were found is the assumed firing position, from where the firing took place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a hypothetical question put by the Prosecutor during the course of today's questioning. I think that this is just a question of a great misunderstanding. I did not talk about drawn bullet-path directions. I talked about the place where the dots were where allegedly there were scattered casings. And on the small hill were the bodies that had lay there previously. I said that from that direction, which was semi-circular, if the firing came from there, all the directions would practically be parallel. So the wounds would be here. Or if the persons were facing the firing persons, then they would be in the chest or in the abdomen, the wounds. Or if they were turned to them in the back, then the bullet paths would go from the back and perhaps a bit upward. I emphasise that. However, during the autopsy, we found -- we found bullet-path directions from all sides. So it wasn't only from one side. There were injuries from top to the bottom and from the bottom to the top and laterally, and on the basis of the sketch that was shown today, I said that that was impossible. I did not talk about the sketch from my testimony yesterday. I talked about the sketch that Mr. Saxon showed me today, that I saw here on the screen. But I made this reservation: I said that for me, this cannot be evidence of anything for me as a doctor. But even if it were so, that that was simply impossible. So that is my answer. I think that we understand each other now. There was a bit of a misunderstanding, wasn't there, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just for the record, I remember that the witness had answered to my question referring to bullet paths, bottom of page 7, leading to page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, Mr. Saxon questioned you at length about what you wore. You gave these explanations. I am not going to examine you about that again. But since you had a jacket on, did you dress expecting that in the months of January you would be spending some time outdoors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dressed so that I would not feel cold when I'm out in the field, and that is normal dressing for the month of January. I had a jacket and perhaps I had a sweater and a shirt. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He wanted to compare that to the multi-layered clothing that you found during the autopsy. Your conclusions in relation to these multiple layers of clothing, were they not that these persons did that or, rather, had these multiple layers of clothing because they were staying outdoors for a long time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could these persons have had multiple layers of clothing if they were sitting in their homes by the fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you entered a house where there was some kind of heating, any kind, even an ordinary fire in the middle of the room, would I have kept your jacket on or would you have taken it off?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always take my jacket off when I enter a house where there is heating, where it's warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are at the time now for the break. We will take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, did you complete your labour during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I did not complete it, Your Honour. I'm about halfway through, it and I'm continuing as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will all be indebted to you at the end. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, Judge Marinkovic was forced by this shooting to leave Racak on the 15th. On the following day, on the 16th, the chief of mission William Walker arrived there with his group. Was it possible to manipulate the bodies in between that time from when Judge Marinkovic was forced to leave due to firing until Walker arrived with his group on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's speculative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's asking the witness to speculate. Ask the questions which he can answer as a matter of fact or relying on his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, based on your expertise or based on your knowledge of facts, can you tell us whether it was possible to manipulate the bodies in the meantime between the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Those are matters you can properly address us on in your final address. The witness can't help you very much in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will remind the witness that he has explained, as a forensic expert, that it was impossible for the hats to remain on the heads of those people who had fallen down. Skull caps. Some of these people were even shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, that Professor Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I explained that twice already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So somebody had to subsequently put on those caps -- on. Is that your expert conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a conclusion I draw based on my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's leading. It's speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think you should leave all those matters to us, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, did you say indeed that it was impossible for a cap to remain on the head after an injury of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that point to the fact that it was subsequently put on, the cap?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're moving into an area of diminishing returns. Diminishing returns are setting in. If you do not have any proper questions of the witness, then we'll bring the re-examination to an end. I think you misunderstand, in any event, the purpose of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think I understand that fully, but in the cross-examination of Mr. Saxon, Professor Dobricanin stated that it was possible to tamper with the bodies, to manipulate them, because they were unable to conduct any examination all the way up until the 18th. Therefore, I attempted to illustrate that with the specific example and for him to tell us whether it was possible that the bodies were tampered with. So this has to do with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, is it your view that the bodies might have been tampered with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, tampering with bodies was quite possible. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on all the information, based on all facts noticed, the skull caps, ladies in black inside the mosque, and several other elements I have mentioned during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, you were shown here a video footage for which -- Mr. Saxon said that it was footage of a house on fire. Based on what I could see, it wasn't really a house but, rather, a shed shouldering. And you were shown this due to the fact -- due to the statement that you gave that there was no shelling. I will not ask for this footage to be shown again, but please tell us this: Were you able to see in that video clip any indicators of there being shelling prior to that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was obviously a house on fire. There was nothing specific about that. That could have been a house in a Serb village or in the Albanian village. There is nothing to show that that was a house in the village of Racak. I didn't see anything resembling that when I was in Racak myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was did you notice any marks of shelling in that footage.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left side, on the left wall of the house I didn't see anything, and the picture was quite blurred as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon also showed you the footage of the weapons uncovered in Racak, and as he himself said, there were many weapons there. In view of the fact that there was shooting in Racak even after those weapons were collected, meaning on the 15th and the 16th and the 17th and the 18th, could we conclude that there was much -- that there were much more weapons there than the police managed to seize on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon asked you something about fingerprinting the weapons. Please tell us briefly. Danica Marinkovic came on the 15th when the weapons were still in Racak and she was forced to leave. Is it customary for the fingerprinting to -- of weapons to be carried out right there at the site or later on once the weapons are taken away?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a procedure regulating how the weapons are to be collected in order to avoid contamination with new fingerprints. Otherwise, this test is not done at the site but, rather, in laboratories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that that was quite an unrestful period, sort of a state of emergency, would it have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "In view of the fact" sounds like we're getting ready for another leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the rest of it. Let's hear the rest of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, was it typical, was it a regular procedure in cases where there was a conflict between the police on the one hand and the armed terrorists on the other hand or members of the KLA to take prints on the weapons discovered there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember that wasn't the job of the people working in my institute. That was done only in the cases where we had terrorists who were arrested with the weapons in the course of the combat. Then fingerprinting would be done, both of them and the weapons. Otherwise, that was not a typical procedure as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, that does seem rather odd. In a case like this where you have 40 bodies and you are to take fingerprints from every one of these bodies and there's a dispute about whether this was a massacre or a combat and there are weapons, does it not seem to you absolutely obvious to carry out a comparison between the fingerprints on the weapons and the fingerprints of the deceased people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Bonomy, I've stated previously that I'm not aware whether the weapons were fingerprinted. It is possible that it was done, but this is outside of our regular work, and I normally never received such results and was not interested in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dobricanin, Mr. Saxon asked you whether Judge Marinkovic was able to interview witnesses. Now, I'm asking you this in relation to that: Once you managed to enter Racak on the 18th, was there a single witness there who could have given a statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day in Racak I did not see a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, yesterday Mr. Saxon showed you a photograph of a boy killed in Racak. Did you have occasion to listen to the testimony of the German journalist Bo Adam who investigated the circumstances under which this boy was killed and made interviews with his family?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it only partially because I had to leave my house when the testimony was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did you see that the family actually explained that the boy had been killed by a bullet fired from the other side of the valley as the family fled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boy had only one wound which -- and the bullet could have been fired from anywhere. It is likely that the boy was on a slope, was on an uphill terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. You were shown a number of photographs here depicting several bodies, especially in the gully, and you were constantly asked to see that there was a certain number, several bodies and so on. Could you please very briefly tell us what is the procedure of establishing identity of persons shown in such photographs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally would never take it upon myself to identify bodies based on such photographs where the bodies are in such position that you can't really see much. This was done in a very approximate manner that has no value in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Just a few more general questions which are related to what Mr. Saxon asked you. In the beginning of the cross-examination, you stated that you had no problems with Albanians after having lived in Kosovo and Metohija for many years.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware whether -- do you know whether Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo had any problems caused by the behaviour of Albanian separatists?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that based on my work because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This certainly was not a topic that I raised during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The ruling is that this doesn't arise, Mr. Milosevic, from cross-examination, so ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noted down the answer of Professor Dobricanin given yesterday to Mr. Saxon where he stated that he personally had no problems with the Albanians. This is why I asked him whether he knew whether Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija did have problems with Albanian separatists. This occurred during cross-examination. This is the answer he gave in the course of cross-examination, and I assume that he himself remembers that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we should move on, Mr. Milosevic, to another question. You're already spending far too long in this re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I have no further questions stemming from the cross-examination except the one that I put you earlier and which had to do with what Mr. Saxon was verifying, namely the exact date when the fingerprints were taken and whether it is indicated in all documents that this was done after the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, how far --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- have you reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have simply -- sorry, Your Honour. I have finished my aide-memoire. It needs to be printed out, copies made and brought down here. I assume that will take a few minutes. My printer that I'm connected to is on the third floor of the building. I can tell the Chamber that about half of the -- half of the fingerprint cards bear no date at all and the other half bear the date 20 January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bear no date at all at the very back, but they nonetheless have the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the bottom part the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how soon could you have the aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As soon as I hit print, Your Honour, then we can ask a staff -- well, I will send it to Ms. Dicklich and she will get it printed out. I assume it will take just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can deal with the admissibility of tab 5, which we reserved, while we're waiting. But I don't remember that the content of tab 5 was put to the witness except for the picture. So if that is the intention of the accused there would be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I stopped my cross-examination before I had a chance to deal with tab 5 just due to the fact that so much time was passing. So I did not address it with the witness. I just want to bring to the Chamber's attention that tab 5 as presented to this witness provides no source of where it comes from. However, the Prosecution has found this material on a website called Srpska Mreza, Serbian network, and I simply wanted to bring that to the Trial Chamber's attention before a decision is made regarding admissibility so the Chamber is aware of the source of that material. And I can provide the Chamber a with a copy of my material as it was found on the website, if the Chamber so wishes. It's part of an article entitled "The Racak File: Truths and Manipulation." And it shows the same photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you confirm that this was not dealt with with this witness? So this does not have to be admitted. We have these kind of pictures already in our exhibits. If you have any observations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked questions -- yes, Mr. Kwon. I referred to tab 5 and just used to show the photographs to the witness. Otherwise, those photographs appeared on several occasions here with respect to Racak. And the witness did answer questions in that regard and explained why it was unnatural or, rather, impossible for the cap that we can see on two of the bodies still be on the head of the person killed, especially on the first photograph, for example, where you can see that the man was hit in the head but his skullcap remains intact on the head. And the Professor gave us detailed explanations as to why that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I guess there would be no opposition from the Prosecution if we admit only that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for that purpose, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll admit the photograph on the second page of tab 5. Mr. Nice, in the age of electronic simultaneity, I rather thought I would have had the benefit of the aide-memoire now, but perhaps you could start the debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in relation to the 24 documents, will you have any questions of the witness? If not, then the witness could be released and we could deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it depends on what we're going to see in the documents, because they haven't been shown. The witness quite clearly said that the fingerprints were taken after the paraffin test, and this is confirmed by the documents that we saw here, that they were taken on the 20th, the fingerprints. Now, I don't know whether there is a single document where -- with a date showing the fingerprints were taken before the 20th. So in that regard whether the witness has something to explain or not because the witness was quite clear in his answer, and he said that the finger -- that the paraffin glove test was first conducted and then the fingerprints came second. And that is something that he stated quite categorically. And this is in fact borne out by the documents, at least the ones we saw here in court. If that is not challenged, then I really do not have any more questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, what are you challenging, if anything, in relation to these -- these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. What am I challenging?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, what is your position if relation to the documents? You just heard what Mr. Milosevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, it is the Prosecution's position that on the face of these documents some at least preliminary fingerprint work was done on these particular victims on the 18th of January. I'm not sure if I'm answering your question, Your Honour. I'm apologising if I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That answers it. That answers it. So we do have a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now have the benefit of Mr. Saxon's work. Mr. Saxon, in relation to the document just produced, am I right in saying that where you have "None" for date on fingerprint card there is the date of the 20th on the first page at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct, Your Honour. The date 20 January 1999 is still recorded on the first page at the bottom, but on the last page of the B/C/S version we see no date, on the fingerprint card itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, do you have any questions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arising from this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no other date but the 20th of January, Mr. Robinson, then I assume that that is sufficient confirmation that Professor Dobricanin spoke correctly and said that the fingerprints were indeed taken on the 20th of January, which is to say after the paraffin glove test traces were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can just respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is certainly no indication on any of these fingerprint forms as to whether this fingerprint work was done before or after any of the gunpowder residue tests. There's simply no information at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have heard submissions from both parties. Let's give that exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will be 857.1 -- 856.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 856.1. With that, Professor, we have concluded your testimony, and we thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us now proceed to the debate on the evidence issue. Mr. Nice, you were at the beginning or near the end of your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before we return to His Honour Judge Bonomy's question which was the last thing that I was asked last night, can I deal with two entirely separate, very short administrative matters to dispose of them. There's a Status Conference tomorrow. If it would assist Chamber, I've got a list of proposals which, rather than file them as a separate filing, I will distribute this afternoon for the saving of time and get it to all parties. Second, and while the evidence of the last witness is still fresh in our memories, the Chamber will recall that Mr. Saxon produced an aide-memoire or a document dealing with names, and His Honour Judge Bonomy suggested that we should try and negotiate with the accused over the topic in the way that we have explained we would have done with any other representative accused. We didn't take long on it then and I don't want to take long on it now save simply to remind the Chamber that there have been several occasions and efforts to cooperate with the accused have been fruitless or when offers have led to nothing coming from him because he doesn't like to get involved in procedural matters -- most notably every Rule 68 invitation to him to get engaged and have parameters changed or something like that have met with no response. And the only occasion that I have met with his associates was on one occasion when there was something they actively wanted from me. Can I respectfully suggest that the Chamber might ask the accused -- rather than us through another fruitless exercise, can the Chamber at some time say to him will you cooperate with us over trying to sort names out because if the answer is yes, we'll get on with it; if the answer is no, if he is obdurate about it, we will know where we stand. Can I return to the immediate issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the accused said that Raif Salihu does not appear on the schedule, he might not have had time to examine all these schedules. We can expect him to go through the schedule and come back with an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We simply shouldn't, if I may say so, we shouldn't -- to use the vernacular, pussyfoot around a problem that the accused creates by his attitude towards these proceedings. In a -- in a functioning court with litigators on both sides representing, the Judge would say to each side well please get together and try and sort this out. And if one of them said no, the Judge would want to know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- I understand exactly you're saying as I explained to Mr. Saxon yesterday, Mr. Nice. But what about on this occasion set out your position as you have done in writing, send it and invite the accused to get an associate to go through this exercise and try to resolve it. Do it in a way -- and then perhaps come back to us. Because at that stage I think I would be happier to become involved in the way that you suggest. But would you be good enough on this occasion to have a specific go at it and see what comes of it. Because the impression I had yesterday from Mr. Milosevic was he was anxious to have it sorted out too. We might see if on this occasion we could make some progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do as Your Honour proposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it is the end of the world, this particular issue, and is one that we should be able to resolve in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without taking too much time, yes. Your Honours, His Honour Judge Bonomy said yesterday and I have it actually in the transcript. I'll read the question. He said: "There are two trials in this court they both involve the same witness or potential witness. The Prosecution position in relation to that witness, I understand, is entirely different in the other case from the position it appears to be taking in relation to the witness in this case." And I was asked whether it's an appropriate position for us to take. And the answer to that question, in my submission, is that it is both appropriate, necessary, and indeed inevitable that we should take the position we do and that there's nothing wrong with that and it's one of the consequences of having several cases involving several different parties to conflicts tried in the same court. It is in fact in many ways I hope to make clear in a couple of sentences and minutes actually rather a good thing. The Chamber will possibly have forgotten, but I must remind you that what is occurring with Jasovic or potentially occurring with Jasovic has already happened in relation to Shukri Buja. He was the witness upon whom the Prosecution relied to deal with the presence of and involvement of the KLA in Racak on the very day of the matters into which we are more particularly inquiring. He was cross-examined but the Prosecution had no reason to doubt him in any way at that stage. He was called in the Limaj case to deal with entirely different evidential matters and he was turned hostile at the request of the Prosecution, thus the Prosecution evincing effectively an expression of view as to him on part of his evidence, namely the evidence he was giving in that case, and that evidence will be available to the accused to deploy at some future date if he wishes to. Now, I mention that right at the outset and weave in this proposition: Where you've got witnesses who may be believable and likely to be telling the truth in part of their evidence and might be more -- might find it more difficult to come clean in respect of other parts of their evidence, it would always be open to an overall prosecuting authority to make rather tactical decisions. To say, well, in case one we would call this witness, but then if we call him in case two and things go badly wrong, well, we'll embarrass case one. And so it could have been the case that counsel in the Limaj case, the other case, could have said that Well, we could see the prospect coming of our having to turn him hostile. Would that damage your case. That would be a rather concerning tactical decision for an overall Prosecution office to make if the Limaj decision was basically that they wanted to call this witness and to get his evidence out even if it meant turning him hostile. It would be concerning because this Chamber, and indeed this accused, would then be deprived of the reality that the witness Shukri Buja was one who was going to be turned hostile because he was vulnerable to the effective views of the Prosecution that that should happen. In that example, of course, the order of events was called first as a witness to be believed and no reason to doubt, and second subject to question in another court. That's the same position as we find now with the witness Jasovic. There was a particular coincidence of timing but in reaction, he was called for the truth of his evidence in the other case and it then became apparent in this case that there will be reason to doubt him. So in each example it's the same order of events. And I mention that simply because one could see at that it might be more difficult if it -- if things happened the other way round. If at any stage it became apparent to the Prosecutor that there might be reasons to doubt a witness it might be more difficult for that witness. Not impossible, but it might be more difficult for that witness to be called in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you invited us, Mr. Nice, I think in relation to him to disregard anything that he was involved in because you were neutralising it with the statements. Is that not -- was that not in relation to him that you said this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't remember putting it in that way but Your Honour's quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly sought to neutralise the statements that he produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in another court he is being defended by the Prosecution against attacks upon him that he was doing exactly the things that you say in this -- in this case he was doing, in other words, torturing his witnesses. Now that's different, is it not? I don't know the detail of the evidence of Shukri Buja in the Limaj case and therefore I'm not in a position to compare them at the moment. But surely we have here an extreme example of a witness that you have to make your mind up about one way or -- otherwise two different Trial Chambers could reach two different conclusions about a man giving evidence in the same court more or less at the same time in relation to whether he tortured witnesses or not because neither perhaps has the full picture. You alone are perhaps in the position to have the full picture and make a judgement. I find this a very invidious position for a Court to be placed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, whether they were defending him on that particular allegation or not I don't know because it depends a little as to what questions were asked in re-examination and whether they were questions of exploration or giving him an opportunity to amplify certain answers, or whether they came with a particular pointed purpose behind them. And we'll have to look at the re-examination if that becomes material. But, Your Honour, although it's an invidious position and a very difficult one it's one that we nevertheless simply have to face given the circumstances in which we all find ourselves in these trials and in this court. And I'll develop that in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's got nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the same could happen in an English court, you're familiar with -- at least that's my understanding -- and a decision would have to be taken with it. At least that's my understanding. And there is no reason in principle why you should regard that as any different from the situation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the position so far as this particular witness then and these particular allegations is concerned is as follows: If the position is as black and white as Your Honour would propose, then it would only be possible for either I in this case to say I'm unable to cross-examine on the basis that he's an unreliable human being or that he's a torturing police officer and that therefore I have to accept without question the material that comes in at his hand; or the other case would have to abandon him. In each case this really being an expression of final view about a witness by counsel prosecuting in one case or the other. Now, can I pause there to invite the Court to consider the underlying approach towards the calling the witnesses. Some of my colleagues, I think, from civil system and perhaps some of them from the United States of America might be more prone than I am ever to express personal views about the credibility of witnesses. My understanding has always been that you can all witnesses and should call witnesses who are capable of being believed; that you're not really there to interpose your own judgement in the matter even if you have one sometimes you do sometimes you don't. What you're not there to do is call witness who is fall outside the parameters of capability of being believed.
