So that you can have the circumstance, which is why I referred earlier to the problems facing witnesses who are involved in these wars and conflicts. You can have the circumstances and it happened -- circumstance it happens often where and witness might be believed in part of his evidence and might be more questionable on another part. We've indeed seen that on the part of several witnesses who I called -- as the Court will remember, I only called for certain limited parts of their testimony making it clear I might not accept what they said about other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you can help me more, Mr. Nice, on this point. We could go on forever on it but I think I have the position very clearly in my mind now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just conclude -- I would like to make two other points. In principle, it is in my submission preferable for the trials to proceed without tactical overall considerations because that would be indeed invidious and to proceed as adversarial trials do when issues arise. And that makes for these uncomfortable possible consequences but it doesn't make it wrong that they happen. In this particular case -- and this brings me immediately to the evidence that the accused now seeks to bring in through this witness. In this particular case when we first heard of him as a source of information, an intervening person between hearsay and the floor of the court, it was essential that I make investigations to find out what I should do next. If I'm presented with a statement produced not by the witness in the witness box but handed to her by a policeman that runs counter to an important part of my case, my duty is to investigate it. I have no choice if I'm to do my job responsibly. And the Court will remember that I declined to cross-examine until I knew what my position was, saying that for all I knew I might have to make concessions. And I didn't want to start the process of cross-examining not knowing where I was going to be challenging or conceding. So that once this material came in, first of all with Marinkovic, Mrs. Marinkovic, and now as is proposed through this witness Jasovic, if he's ever called, my duty is to check it. And I simply cannot say up the system of trial we have well because the officer has been called in another case as a witness of truth I'm in the allowed, for example, to go to these witnesses and say, "Did you say these things to this officer? Were they true?" The consequence of my being in that position is not only that all these 80 statements would have to go in unchallenged as to their content in any way but any such material coming in by any such witness would be beyond my ability under the adversarial system to challenge. With those last two general points, then, the application as repeated by Mr. Kay allows me, I think, a few further points. But can I invite the Chamber to take a step back because we being looking at the adduction of 80, effectively, witness statements. No it's not Your Honour, the tab -- if you go to tab 1 it goes to 57 then 2 goes to 30, so that's 87. Then there is tab 3 and 4 so it's 89. The way the accused explained his application yesterday morning was that he wanted this material in because it indicated or partially indicated things and information that the organs of the Interior had about activities of terrorists in the area of Racak. He went on to say that it showed that there were different names in many of the statements of persons who fell casualty in Racak. He suggested you could paint a clear picture of what happened, and then he linked it to the witness Dobricanin and said you will gain a clear later -- a comprehensive, clear picture. Insofar as the accused was explaining in legal terms what he was hoping to achieve, I think it would be possible to infer from what he said that this material -- that I certainly have not analysed, 89 statements -- will identify KLA-active individuals both in 1998 and indeed because we see the statements go to 1999 and in 1999, and from his own application it may well be although he isn't explicit about it, that this will deal with the alleged KLA involvement of some of those said to have died as innocent civilians by the Prosecution, i.e., there will be further statements of the three or four dealt with specifically through Mrs. Marinkovic. My learned friend Mr. Kay in the afternoon yesterday invited your further consideration, and he said amongst other things the following: He said that there were further names as well as a repetition of names mentioned in the earlier witnesses' materials which were witness statements -- sorry, yes, further names beyond those adduced through Mrs. Marinkovic. And he said as having referred to as having connections with the KLA he said this, then: "It comes down to about 30 of those names in Schedule A fall into category. So they are identified in witness statements taken by Jasovic for 1998 to 1999 for the KLA." So pausing there. If he and the accused are arguing a common theme, it seems that they are putting this material in for the truth of its content to go to show that people in Schedule A were active KLA people. Later Mr. Kay put the matter differently, and he said that the "case concerns the criminal responsibility of the accused and goes to the issue of his state of mind" in that they are official records at the time that have been created or not being created for the issue that we are concerned with. "They are within the system of law-enforcement agencies, and it's right to say," said Mr. Kay, "that the accused would be entitled to rely upon the content of that information to prove matters relevant to the issue concerning his state of mind." He amplified that and pressed on you that he would be entitled to put the material in on that basis, suggesting at the end, having looked at the position with Captain Dragan as he was known, called by the Prosecution, he went on to say that this was material prepared before the indictment unrelated to the case and suggested that that was a classically different type of evidence. So that Your Honour -- I'm sorry to take you through that, but the position I face, I think, despite Mr. Kay's second basis of application, is that this material should go in for the truth of its content. If that's the case, point number one is I really need to know exactly what is being relied on and what is going to be said through this material. It may be different things for different statements, and simply to give me 80 statements -- and it's true as a matter of fact we've been able to find English translations of most or all of these statements overnight, but I haven't gone through them but I really need to know before I consider my position finally about Jasovic what is being relied on and to prove what. But I assume for the balance of what I'm going to say that it is what it appears to be, that the accused and Mr. Kay said could be proved, namely that many people of those said to be innocent civilians are actually KLA activists. And it's with that in mind that I respectfully remind Your Honours of two things. First, there have been the general practice of this Chamber and I drew to your attention one example from His Honour Judge May where he said in terms in the course of the evidence of Helena Ranta that statements weren't typically produced, and he said the same thing in relation to another witness at a later stage when the accused was trying to get in the witness statement of someone who would have given a different account for the death than the account that was being given by the witness in court and he said to the accused that the proper course would you for you to call this witness in which case he could give in his evidence. Meanwhile if you still want to have his statement exhibited he said we'll mark it for identification. He went no further than that. That can be found at page 7914. Picking up on the point raised yesterday about what is the potential legal position of such material, and although I know the Chamber will be familiar with the Appeals Chamber's decision on the admissibility of investigators' evidence, can I remind you of one short paragraph at the end of paragraph 18 where the Appeals Chamber having dealt with the position both in Kordic and in Galic found as follows, and I'll read this slowly: "To avoid any misunderstanding, however, it is perhaps necessary to add that there is nothing in the Galic decision which prevents a written statement given by prospective witnesses to OTP investigators or others for the purposes of legal proceedings being received in evidence notwithstanding its non-compliance with Rule 92 bis, one, where there has been no objection taken to it; or, two, where it is otherwise -- it has otherwise become admissible where, for example, the written statement is asserted to contain a prior statement inconsistent with the witness's evidence." Neither of those exceptions applies here. And the principles advanced by the Appeals Chamber, with which this Chamber will be familiar, in our respectful submission would determine that this material - which is important material, Galic covers this - on an important part of the Prosecution's case should not come in other than by the witnesses being called or if there's a reason not to quality witnesses for example because they're dead and the qualifying conditions that allow the admissibility of such statements be met, only after all those necessary pre-conditions have been met. And so in my respectful submission, these statements that appear to be made for legal proceedings or in the course of some kind of legal process but obviously not for these proceedings, these documents simply do not qualify and should not be allowed into evidence. Your Honours, I'll just see if Mr. Saxon wants to add something but I'm not sure. Thank you. I'll go back to war I started yesterday, with this series of statements that came in through Marinkovic. Now all of these there is no explanation given for not calling the material -- the people concerned live and on such an important issue that is what you, in our respectful submission, must have. If in the event and I'm only saying this to avoid popping up and down, if in the event the Court is prepared to admit 89 statements of this kind without them being clarified as to their purpose, separated out between those that refer to people in the Racak schedule and so on or otherwise, I simply say I'm quite unable to deal with them today or indeed tomorrow, because obviously on a potentially important issue I will have to inquire into them. And that would be another reason -- no. I need say no more than that. Your Honours, unless I can assist further -- I should I suppose say that it doesn't seem to me with great respects to Mr. Kay that his second argument seek to go categorise these as -- in a different class because they simply came to light before the indictment or before this inquiry and not for the purpose of it changes their status. They are still statements made, as it happens, in some kind of judicial or police proceedings. But they are the statements out of court, and they need to meet the various indicia for admissibility of reliability if they're to be admitted. Perhaps, yes, I ought just to emphasise that. I've emphasised it before or made the point before. Where there are serious issues as to the reliability of statements, and this again is dealt with in the ruling of the Appeals Chamber on the admissibility of the investigators' evidence at paragraphs 26 to 31, I think. Where there are serious issues as to the credibility, then of course hearsay evidence should not be admitted. And in our respectful submission the three contrary statements produced in the way that we suggest they were taken, and we've shown they were indeed taken, I hope, are themselves quite sufficient to show that there are indicia of unreliability attached to the work of this police officer and in those circumstances it would simply be not safe -- not be safe to allow them in in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you please go back to paragraph 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- of the Appeals Chamber's decision on the admissibility of investigators' evidence. They cited two circumstances in which statements which did not meet the criteria of Rule 92 bis could nonetheless be admitted. One where there is no objection, and the second one was prior inconsistent statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was that an example of a wider range, the prior inconsistent statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't spell it out in terms, but I wouldn't argue in favour of my argument that is exhaustive. It would seem to be exemplary. I'm not going to try and take a technical advantage of the way they've expressed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, well, we did hear from you already. And Mr. Milosevic -- let us hear from Mr. Milosevic first. I want Mr. Milosevic to clarify the purpose for which he is seeking to adduce these witness statements. Oh, I see we are out of time. There is another case here this afternoon, Mr. Legal Clerk. I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We do have the Limaj case this afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is the Limaj case here this afternoon. Thank you very much. We will have to take the break now, and we are due to continue tomorrow. 8.00 Status Conference, and then 9.00 we'll resume this debate and hear the submissions from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Status Conference is at 8.00, and at 9.00 we will resume the trial, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that we can just continue after the Status Conference. We don't need to have a changeover. Mr. Milosevic, you should have another witness on standby, quite apart from Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Mr. Robinson. Do I have the possibility of saying at least a few sentences by way of explanation why I believe that Mr. Jasovic should be heard and why I believe that is of significance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not now, tomorrow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
